extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, litigants, and others researching or practicing patent law
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation of the doctrine of claim differentiation — the legal principle for interpreting patent claims so that each claim has a distinct scope. Guidance covers when and how the doctrine is applied in prosecution and litigation, its purpose, common misunderstandings, and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that each claim has a unique scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Each claim in a patent is presumed to have a unique scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presumption underlies claim interpretation: no two claims should cover the same subject matter. It promotes clarity and reduces ambiguity across a patent's claim set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims must be more limiting than independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims must be more limiting than the independent claims they refer to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims are interpreted to provide additional specific limitations and thus define a subset of the independent claim. Example given: an independent claim for a bicycle frame with dependent claims specifying materials or handlebar design — the dependent claims should be narrower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not be interpreted to cover identical subject matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims cannot be interpreted to cover the same subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreting two claims as coextensive contradicts the doctrine; claim language should be read so as to avoid rendering one claim redundant with another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should not import limitations from one claim into another
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not import limitations from one claim into another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When construing claims, courts should avoid reading a limitation appearing only in a dependent claim into the broader independent claim, because that would improperly narrow the independent claim and undermine claim differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the doctrine in patent examination and litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine is primarily applied in patent litigation and during the patent examination process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners use it to argue for broader interpretations of claims (e.g., in defending against infringement) or to support particular constructions during prosecution. It is a tool during claim construction disputes before courts or examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose: promote clarity and prevent ambiguity in claim sets
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine is designed to promote clarity and prevent ambiguity in patent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By treating claims as having distinct meanings, the doctrine helps delineate the scope of protection and reduces interpretive overlap that could create uncertainty for patent owners and third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on broadening dependent claims by importing independent-claim features
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims cannot be broadened to include features from independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrary to some misunderstandings, dependent claims are not meant to be used to enlarge the scope of an independent claim by importing elements; they are intended to add limitations, not broaden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to claim construction and other doctrines (e.g., Doctrine of Equivalents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim differentiation is a principle that guides the claim construction process and is distinct from doctrines like the Doctrine of Equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While claim differentiation directs how literal claim language is read (ensuring distinct scopes), the Doctrine of Equivalents addresses infringement when an accused product falls outside the literal claim language but is equivalent in substance. Use claim differentiation when construing literal scope; use equivalence doctrines for non-literal infringement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical examples illustrating proper application
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical examples demonstrate how dependent claims should form narrower subsets of independent claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an independent claim for a 'vehicle' and a dependent claim for an 'electric vehicle' — the dependent claim must be interpreted as a specific subset. Another example: bicycle frame with dependent claims for material or handlebar design. These examples show how to read dependent claims as adding limitations.
